summary: Contains the text of the agreement between ISOC and the IETF on one side and ISO/IEC JTC1/SC6 on the other, covering cooperative development of the IS-IS routing protocol. It defines the scope of each group's work, asks IANA to maintain an IS-IS registry, and sets collaboration guidelines. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two groups both worked on the same routing system. This memo records the written agreement on who handles which part and how they share the work.

subtitle: The written deal that split IS-IS routing work between the IETF and the ISO/IEC standards committee.

tldr.problem: The IS-IS routing protocol came from ISO/IEC JTC1/SC6 but was being extended for the Internet by the IETF, so the two bodies needed rules to avoid overlapping or conflicting work.
tldr.mechanism: The agreement defines Core IS-IS Mechanisms and Internet-specific Extensions, gives the IETF the second and JTC1 the rest, asks IANA to hold an IS-IS TLV registry for now, and sets collaboration rules.
tldr.outcome: It is a process document, not a protocol. It has been updated by RFC 6233.

today: RFC 3563 is an Informational RFC that has been updated by RFC 6233; it has not been obsoleted. It records a process agreement, not a protocol.

sections.title: Why the Agreement Exists
sections.content:
RFC 3563 contains the text of an agreement signed between ISOC/IETF and ISO/IEC JTC1/SC6. The subject is the IS-IS intra-domain routing protocol (ISO/IEC 10589). The RFC says IS-IS was originally developed in JTC1/SC6 and has been successfully deployed in the Internet for several years.

SC6 is responsible for maintaining the IS-IS standard. The IETF IS-IS Working Group is chartered to develop extensions for use within the scope of the Internet. The agreement documents how both will develop IS-IS from here on.

The document is an annexe to a broader cooperative agreement. It is dated 2003-01-28, and its signatures are dated March 2003.
sections.eli5: Two clubs both wanted to improve the same game. They wrote down who makes which rules so they would not step on each other.

sections.title: Core Mechanisms and Internet Extensions
sections.content:
Core IS-IS Mechanisms are the heart of the protocol as specified in ISO/IEC 10589. They include the PDU framework with TLVs, PDU encapsulation, the adjacency state machine, DIS election, initial LSP synchronization via CSNP exchange, asynchronous LSP flooding, LSP database maintenance, and the topology abstraction.

Internet-specific IS-IS Extensions fall within the IETF's work scope, including any routing or forwarding technology the IETF decides to work on, such as IPv4 or IPv6 routing, MPLS or Generalized MPLS. To qualify, an extension must meet one of three tests: it does not modify the core and does not change operation of non-IP implementations; or it adds supplementary mechanisms that are not generally applicable to non-IP implementations and do not affect their compatibility; or it is a de facto implementation agreement not generally applicable to non-IP implementations.

Adding new TLVs or sub-TLVs that do not alter the core algorithms in a way that affects interoperability with non-IP or dual implementations is not treated as modifying the core.
sections.eli5: The engine of the game belongs to the old club. Extra parts that only matter for the Internet belong to the new club, as long as they do not break the engine for everyone else.

sections.title: Who Standardizes What
sections.content:
JTC1 SHALL NOT standardize any Internet-specific IS-IS Extensions, and the IETF MAY, subject to its standards process. Extensions made in the IETF that need standardization but are not Internet-specific SHOULD go to JTC1, and the IETF SHALL NOT publish them other than as Informational RFCs.

Extensions sent from the IETF to JTC1 use the JTC1 fast track procedure. To keep quality up, the IETF applies the Proposed Standard procedures of RFC 2026 to them. Standards-track IS-IS documents MUST include a section explaining why they count as Internet-specific.

Unclear cases are decided case by case, by agreement between the IETF Routing Area Directors or the IETF liaison to JTC1/SC6 and the JTC1/SC6 secretariat.

To submit to JTC1, an ISIS WG chair or Routing Area director emails the JTC1 secretariat with the number of the Informational RFC, which must already be published, and asks for fast-track processing. Going the other way, a JTC1 specification can be offered to the IETF by submitting it as an Internet Draft and asking the RFC Editor to publish it as an Informational RFC.
sections.eli5: If a new part is only for the Internet, the new club may build it. If it is for everyone, it goes to the old club, and the new club has to double-check its homework first.

sections.title: The IS-IS TLV Registry
sections.content:
Until JTC1 provides a registry service, IANA is asked to temporarily maintain an IS-IS TLV codepoint registry. The range of values is 0-255 and the initial state is to be synchronized with RFC 3359. Each allocation must be approved by a designated expert assigned by the IESG.

The IETF SHALL keep JTC1/SC6 informed of allocations, and JTC1/SC6 SHALL refer allocation requests arising in its constituencies to the IANA process. When JTC1 notifies that it can take over, allocation authority transfers to JTC1, and IANA MAY keep the registry for information.

The IETF may also ask IANA to hold other IS-IS registries for name spaces internal to Internet-specific extensions.
sections.eli5: There is one big list of numbered labels. For now a librarian keeps it, and later the old club can take it back.

sections.title: Collaboration Guidelines
sections.content:
The IETF SHALL tell the chairman and secretariat of ISO JTC 1/SC 6 about new IS-IS work items, and JTC1/SC6 SHALL tell the IETF Routing Area directors and ISIS WG chairs. This can be done by email or through appointed liaison representatives.

Members of SC6 are welcome to review any IS-IS-related IETF document and send comments to the ISIS WG list, its chairs, the Routing Area directors or the IESG. JTC1 is encouraged to ask for IETF review of its own IS-IS work by submitting it as an informational Internet Draft. The IETF may ask JTC1 to circulate comments among the National Bodies and Liaison Organizations involved.

On security, the RFC says this type of non-protocol document does not directly affect the security of the Internet.
sections.eli5: Each club promises to tell the other about new projects and to let the other peek at drafts and give advice.
